The lamellae are made of good steel or phosphor bronze, which gives them good spring and resonance. The body usually has a resonance chamber inside, hollowed out to deepen and warm the timbre. On some instruments the edge of the body is set with leather or cloth to prevent wear, and the lamellae are fixed to the body with metal clamps for stability and durability.

Its range lies in the low frequencies, its tone is steady and full of body, and every pluck leaves a long after-ring. The hollow body amplifies the sound wave, giving a thick, penetrating tone. Against the clear arpeggios of the traditional piano the bass likembe sounds heavier and more distant; against the double bass its tone has a warmer folk colour. Its idiophonic character lets it create a meditative atmosphere: the timbre is neither too bright and harsh nor too dark, but keeps a moderate transparency and depth of resonance, which suits mysterious, calming musical moods.

The bass likembe is a traditional percussion instrument from eastern and central Africa, belonging to the thumb-piano family. The instrument has a wooden body and metal lamellae, and the player sounds it by plucking the lamellae with both thumbs. Its shape is a flat rectangle, easy to hold while playing. Its range is wide and deep, its timbre warm and full of body, with a long resonance. It is used mainly in world music, meditation music, film scores and modern experimental composition, where it builds a mysterious, meditative atmosphere; it is an important instrument for filling out a band's bass register.

Different parts and different amounts of force give different timbres. In practice, first check the correct holding position, then, once the basic way of sounding it is secure, work on rhythm patterns and melody. Pluck the strings with a fingertip or a pick, and watch the angle and force of the attack.
拇指琴屬撥奏體鳴器（122.1），源自辛巴威紹納人。非洲各地存在此類樂器數千年，: The thumb piano is a plucked idiophone (122.1), coming from the Shona people of Zimbabwe. Instruments of this kind have existed in various parts of Africa for thousands of years: the early lamellae were bamboo, and metal lamellae came later; the west coast of Africa had wooden and bamboo lamellae about three thousand years ago, and metal lamellae appeared in the Zambezi valley about thirteen hundred years ago. Metal-lamella instruments spread across Africa and took different forms and social uses in Zimbabwe, Mozambique and elsewhere. In the mid-1950s the ethnomusicologist Hugh Tracey designed and marketed the kalimba on the basis of the mbira, which let it spread beyond Africa; in 2020 its making and playing were entered on UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage.
